extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, scholars, and statesmen (early modern/learned public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the value, conduct, and errors of learning and learned men — i.e., what good learning should do and what vices in studies and scholars discredit learning. Aimed at evaluating scholarship, education, and the behaviour of scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning as remedy for irresolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning ministereth...greater strength of medicine or remedy than it offereth cause of indisposition or infirmity: it teacheth when and upon what ground to resolve, yea, and how to carry things in suspense, without prejudice, till they resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether learning strengthens decision-making: teaches appropriate grounds for resolution, and how to suspend judgment safely. Examples given: errors of Clement VII, Cicero, Phocion, Ixion, Cato II. Anti-pattern: learning that produces only confusion and irresolution without tools for prudent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish demonstrative from conjectural
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning teacheth what things are in their nature demonstrative, and what are conjectural, and as well the use of distinctions and exceptions, as the latitude of principles and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether scholarship clearly separates demonstrable truths from conjectures, uses distinctions and exceptions appropriately, and recognizes limits of principles. Anti-pattern: presenting conjectures as demonstrations or failing to signal degrees of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical examples as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: These medicines it conveyeth into men’s minds much more forcibly by the quickness and penetration of examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer learning that leverages vivid historical examples to teach practical lessons and to deter error. Examples cited (Clement VII, Cicero, Phocion) illustrate how examples correct faulty dispositions. Anti-pattern: abstract generalities without illustrative cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning fosters industriousness, not sloth
rubrics_metrics.description: Only learned men love business as an action according to nature... taking pleasure in the action itself... so that of all men they are the most indefatigable, if it be towards any business which can hold or detain their mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the conceit that learning disposes men to idleness. Evaluate whether learned persons take pleasure in work for its own sake rather than for wages or honour. Anti-pattern: assuming a studious life equals laziness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning makes good use of leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: The most active or busy man... hath many vacant times of leisure... the question is but how those spaces and times of leisure shall be filled and spent... no man need doubt that learning will expel business, but rather it will keep and defend the possession of the mind against idleness and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether study is presented as a valuable use of spare time that preserves the mind from idleness. Example: Demosthenes’ lamp-light vs Æschines. Anti-pattern: portraying study as extravagant consumption of indispensable business time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning supports reverence for laws and government
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning doth make the minds of men gentle, generous, manageable, and pliant to government; whereas ignorance makes them churlish, thwart, and mutinous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the effects of learning are claimed to promote civility and obedience rather than subversion. Anti-pattern: asserting learning necessarily undermines polity or breeds sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material fortune of scholars not a disproof of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Derogations...from the fortune or condition of learned men, are either in respect of scarcity of means, or in respect of privateness of life and meanness of employments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use poverty or lack of worldly advancement as evidence against the value of learning. Historical and philosophical arguments defend poverty of scholars as compatible with virtue. Anti-pattern: devaluing knowledge because its practitioners are poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private/contemplative life is not disgraceful
rubrics_metrics.description: The privateness or obscureness... of contemplative men... is a theme so common to extol a private life, not taxed with sensuality and sloth, in comparison and to the disadvantage of a civil life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims about reclusiveness: private life can be consistent with virtue and useful public effects; absence from public office is not inherently shameful. Anti-pattern: equating privacy with cowardice or irrelevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanness of employments (teaching youth) is honorable
rubrics_metrics.description: That the government of youth is commonly allotted to them... this age, because it is the age of least authority, it is transferred to the disesteeming of those employments... But how unjust this traducement is...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not despise educational roles; evaluate whether the work of tutors and schoolmasters is recognized as foundational and fitting. Anti-pattern: contempt for teaching because it is 'low' or little-authoritative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studies influence manners (Abeunt studia in mores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon an attentive and indifferent review... I for my part cannot find any disgrace to learning can proceed from the manners of learned men; not inherent to them as they are learned; except it be a fault... that they contend sometimes too far to bring things to perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how studies shape character. Evaluate whether learned dispositions produce beneficial gentleness or problematic excessive exactness. Anti-pattern: blaming learning itself for personal vices without distinguishing individual temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impractical perfectionism
rubrics_metrics.description: They contend sometimes too far to bring things to perfection, and to reduce the corruption of manners to honesty of precepts or examples of too great height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique learning that sets impractical, Platonic standards that do more harm than good in civic life. Look for caveats and tempering examples (Solon, Plato, Cicero). Anti-pattern: endorsing prescriptions unsuited to actual human capacities and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly loyalty to public good over self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: They have esteemed the preservation, good, and honour of their countries or masters before their own fortunes or safeties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value learning that produces counsel and action oriented toward commonwealth or sovereign welfare even at personal cost. Example: Demosthenes, Seneca. Anti-pattern: scholars chiefly seeking personal advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply learning appropriately to particular persons
rubrics_metrics.description: They fail sometimes in applying themselves to particular persons... the largeness of their mind can hardly confine itself to dwell in the exquisite observation or examination of the nature and customs of one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether learned counsel is suitably adapted to individual circumstances and persons. Distinguish between inability and deliberate choice to refrain from intrusive speculation about individuals. Anti-pattern: speculative efforts to 'work' or manipulate persons under guise of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decency and discretion in small acts
rubrics_metrics.description: They do many times fail to observe decency and discretion in their behaviour and carriage... the vulgar sort of capacities do make a judgment of them in greater matters by that which they find wanting in them in smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scholars on ordinary deportment as well as intellect; small lapses may unduly tarnish reputation. Example: Themistocles’ remark and Plato on Socrates. Anti-pattern: ignoring mundane manners because of intellectual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flattery and patronage as the rule of books
rubrics_metrics.description: This gross and palpable flattery whereunto many not unlearned have abased and abused their wits and pens... the modern dedication of books and writings, as to patrons, to be commended... books ought to have no patrons but truth and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writings dedicated to truth and reason, not flattery of patrons. Criticize excessive dedications and servile patronage that degrade intellectual integrity. Nuance: prudent submissions for necessity/advantage are sometimes defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical submissions for necessity are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: These and the like courses may deserve rather reprehension than defence... these and the like applications, and stooping to points of necessity and convenience, cannot be disallowed; for though they may have some outward baseness, yet in a judgment truly made they are to be accounted submissions to the occasion and not to the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize pragmatic compromises—e.g., seeking patrons or yielding to power—may be excused when necessary for survival or effect, provided they do not corrupt truth. Anti-pattern: blanket moralizing that forbids all practical concessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastical/delicate learning: study of words over matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The first distemper of learning, when men study words and not matter... men began to hunt more after words than matter—more after the choiceness of the phrase... than after the weight of matter, worth of subject, soundness of argument, life of invention, or depth of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize substantive inquiry over rhetorical elegance. Eloquence may aid communication but is contemptible when it substitutes for genuine thought. Anti-pattern: valuing ornate style above truth and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentious learning: novelty and strict positions
rubrics_metrics.description: He assigneth two marks and badges of suspected and falsified science: the one, the novelty and strangeness of terms; the other, the strictness of positions, which of necessity doth induce oppositions, and so questions and altercations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of learning that prizes novelty of terminology and breeds endless oppositions and disputes. Favor universality, breadth of reading, and inquiry grounded in useful subjects. Anti-pattern: cultivating hair-splitting controversies for their own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unprofitable subtilty and endless distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: This same unprofitable subtility or curiosity is of two sorts... or in the manner or method of handling of a knowledge, which... framed objections, and to those objections, solutions... mostly not confutations, but distinctions... Quæstionum minutiis scientiarum frangunt soliditatem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods that build harmonious, supporting parts rather than ones that tear axioms apart into endless cavils. Evaluate whether an approach advances usable, combined knowledge vs. producing merely technical distinctions. Anti-pattern: method of perpetual exceptions and hair-splitting that undermines the 'bond' of a science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning must represent truth; avoid imposture
rubrics_metrics.description: The third vice or disease of learning, which concerneth deceit or untruth... This vice therefore brancheth itself into two sorts; delight in deceiving and aptness to be deceived; imposture and credulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scholarship for honesty and veracity. Beware willful imposture (deceiving) and naive credulity (accepting falsehood). Examples: miraculous hagiography, falsified natural histories. Anti-pattern: recording or promoting known falsehoods or romances as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism in historical and natural reports
rubrics_metrics.description: This facility of credit... either a belief of history... or else of matter of art and opinion... experience and inconvenience... ecclesiastical history... natural history... fraught with much fabulous matter, a great part not only untried, but notoriously untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require critical scrutiny of historical and natural claims; separate well-attested facts from prodigies and popular fables. Follow Aristotle’s example of segregating prodigies into special accounts to avoid contaminating general knowledge. Anti-pattern: mixing doubtful marvels indiscriminately with reliable observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive reliance on dubious arts and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: This facility of credit which is yielded to arts and opinions... either when too much belief is attributed to the arts themselves, or to certain authors in any art... the sciences... astrology, natural magic, and alchemy... the ends or pretences are noble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about excessive trust in speculative arts (astrology, magic, alchemy) and uncritical deference to authorities. Evaluate methods and claims on evidence rather than pedigree. Anti-pattern: accepting occult arts or single-author doctrines without validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate rarities/prodigies from general doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle... hath mingled it sparingly with any vain or feigned matter; and yet on the other side hath cast all prodigious narrations... into one book, excellently discerning that matter of manifest truth... was not to be mingled or weakened with matter of doubtful credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work distinguishes between ordinary, evidential observations and rare/unverified reports; keep general principles free from contamination by doubtful anecdotes. Anti-pattern: integrating prodigies into the main body of doctrine so as to weaken credible claims.
